```html
		<script>
        var camera ;
		var controls ;         // Declare global variables
		var scene ;
		var cube ;
		var sphere ;
		var line ;
		var objNames = ["Earth_Orbit", "Mars_orbit", "Mercury_Orbit", "Venus_Orbit"] ;
		var objSizes = [0.2, 0.17, 0.07, 0.2] ;
		var objColors = [0x0066FF, 0xCC3333, 0xFF0000, 0xFFFFFF] ;
		var curObj = new THREE.Object3D();
		var celestialBody ;
		var heavenlyBodies = [] ;
		
		function init() {
            camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera( 75, window.innerWidth / window.innerHeight, 0.1, 1000 );

			controls = new THREE.TrackballControls( camera );
				controls.rotateSpeed = 1.0;
				controls.zoomSpeed = 1.2;
				controls.panSpeed = 0.8;
				controls.noZoom = false;
				controls.noPan = false;
				controls.staticMoving = true;
				controls.dynamicDampingFactor = 0.3;
				controls.keys = [ 65, 83, 68 ];
				controls.addEventListener( 'change', render );
				
			scene = new THREE.Scene();
								
            renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer();
            renderer.setSize( window.innerWidth/2, window.innerHeight/2);
            document.body.appendChild( renderer.domElement );
			

		    var j = 0 ;
		//  Here comes the Sun!
			var geometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry( 0.6, 16, 16 );
			var material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial( {color: 0xFFFF00, wireframe: false} );
            sphere = new THREE.Mesh( geometry, material );
			scene.add( sphere );
			
			var light = new THREE.PointLight( 0xff0000, 1, 100 );
            light.position.set( 0, 0, 0 );           
            scene.add( light );                       // currently no effect
			
			for (i = 0; i < 4; i++) { // Add the inner planets.
		
			 geometry = new THREE.SphereGeometry( objSizes[j], 16, 16 );
		     material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial( {color: objColors[j], wireframe: false} );
             sphere = new THREE.Mesh( geometry, material );
			 
			 sphere.name = objNames[i] ;
             scene.add( sphere );
			 
			  j = j + 1 ;
			} 
			camera.position.z = 5;
			
		//	console.log(scene) ;
		
		}
		</script>

   		  function animate() {
				requestAnimationFrame( animate );
				controls.update();
				updatePosition() ;
			}

     function populate_table(rowNum,name,argP,meanA,ecc,inc,sma,raan,per) {
	     console.log(rowNum + "  " + name + "," + argP + "," + meanA + "," + ecc);
		 var cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c1"; console.log(cellID);
		 cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c1"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = name;
         cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c2"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = argP;
         cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c3"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = meanA;

         cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c5"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = inc;
         cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c6"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = sma;
         cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c7"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = raan;
         cellID = "r" + rowNum + "c8"    ; document.getElementById(cellID).textContent = per;
	  
	 }

		   field = result.graph[i];

		   //smA,oI,aP,oE,aN,mAe,Sidereal
             celestialBody = new Trajectory(field.name.value,

									 field.inclination.value,
									 field.argPerigee.value,
									 field.eccentricity.value,
```

```html
		  "graph": "@graph",
		  "type": "@type",
		  "value": "@value"
		 };
		
		jsonld.compact(data, context, function(err, compacted) {
       console.log(JSON.stringify(compacted, null, 2));
    $( ".container" ).append("<pre> " + JSON.stringify(compacted, null, 2) + "</pre>");
     });
}) ;
```

## File: OntologyDrivenOrrery/OrbitalPropagator.js
```javascript
// Constructor to generate objects that identify orbital elements.
function Trajectory(name, smA,oI,aP,oE,aN,mAe,Sidereal){

   this.name = name                          // name the object
   this.smA = smA                            // semi major axis
   this.oI = oI * 0.01745329                 // orbital inclination --> convert degrees to radians
   this.aP = aP * 0.01745329                 // argument of Perigee --> convert degrees to radians
   this.oE = oE                              // orbital eccentricity
   this.aN = aN * 0.01745329                 // ascending node --> convert degrees to radians
   this.period = Sidereal                    // siderial period as a multiple of Earth's orbital period
   this.epochMeanAnomaly = mAe * 0.01745329  // mean anomaly at epoch 
   this.trueAnomoly = 0                      // initialize to mean anomaly at epoch
   this.position = [0,0,0] 
   this.time = 0 
}
//--------------------------------------------
//        Trajectory Propagator
//--------------------------------------------
Trajectory.prototype.propagate = function(uA){
// Purpose: Determine a position on an orbital trajectory based on a true anomoly.
// Used by the traceOrbits function to draw the orbits.
var pos = [] ;
var xdot; var ydot; var zdot;            // velocity coordinates
var theta = uA;                          // Update true anomaly.
var smA = this.smA;                      // Semi-major Axis
var oI =  this.oI ;                      // Orbital Inclination
var aP = this.aP ;                       // Get the object's orbital elements.
var oE = this.oE;                        // Orbital eccentricity
var aN = this.aN ;                       // ascending Node
var sLR = smA * (1 - oE^2) ;             // Compute Semi-Latus Rectum.
var r = sLR/(1 + oE * Math.cos(theta));  // Compute radial distance.

// Compute position coordinates pos[0] is x, pos[1] is y, pos[2] is z
pos[0] = r * (Math.cos(aP + theta) * Math.cos(aN) - Math.cos(oI) * Math.sin(aP + theta) * Math.sin(aN)) ;  
pos[1] = r * (Math.cos(aP + theta) * Math.sin(aN) + Math.cos(oI) * Math.sin(aP + theta) * Math.cos(aN)) ;
pos[2] = r * (Math.sin(aP + theta) * Math.sin(oI)) ;

return pos ;
}
//-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
function traceOrbits()  
	{  // Generate line segments from points around the trajectory of the orbiting objects.
	   // Trace the orbits for the following array of objects.
	  var geometry ;
	  var material = new THREE.LineBasicMaterial({color: 0xCCCCFF });  
	console.log("Entering traceOrbits " + heavenlyBodies.length) ;
	for (var hB in heavenlyBodies) {
	   var orbPos = [];
	   var j = 0;                // Initialize the orbit index, which will build the orbIndices list. 
	   geometry = new THREE.Geometry();   // Create an object for each orbit.
	   var i = 0.0 ;
	   while (i <= 6.28) {
	     orbPos = heavenlyBodies[hB].propagate(i) ;   // Propagate the orbits.
		 // Store the vertices.
		 geometry.vertices.push(new THREE.Vector3(orbPos[0].toFixed(2), orbPos[1].toFixed(2), orbPos[2].toFixed(2)));

		 i = i + 0.0785
		 j = j + 1 ;          // Increment the orbit index.
        }
	    line = new THREE.Line(geometry, material);
		var orbitName = heavenlyBodies[hB].name.value + "_trace" ; 
		line.name = orbitName ;

		scene.add(line);
		console.log("line name  " + orbitName ) ;
	 }
	 console.log("Exiting traceOrbits") ;
  };
/*-------------------------------------------------------------*
 *   Utility functions for true, eccentric and mean anomalies  *
 *-------------------------------------------------------------*/
 function trueToEccentricAnomaly(e,f) {
// http://mmae.iit.edu/~mpeet/Classes/MMAE441/Spacecraft/441Lecture19.pdf slide 7 
 var eccentricAnomaly = 2* Math.atan(Math.sqrt((1-e)/(1+e))* Math.tan(f/2));

	return eccentricAnomaly ;
}
function meanToEccentricAnomaly (e, M) {
// Solves for eccentric anomaly, E from a given mean anomaly, M
// and eccentricty, e.  Performs a simple Newton-Raphson iteration
// Code derived from Matlab scripts written by Richard Rieber, 1/23/2005
// http://www.mathworks.com/matlabcentral/fileexchange/6779-calce-m
   var tol = 0.0001;  // tolerance
   var eAo = M;       // initialize eccentric anomaly with mean anomaly
   var ratio = 1;     // set ratio higher than the tolerance
while (Math.abs(ratio) > tol) {
    var f_E = eAo - e * Math.sin(eAo) - M;
    var f_Eprime = 1 - e * Math.cos(eAo);
    ratio = f_E / f_Eprime;
    if (Math.abs(ratio) > tol) {
        eAo = eAo - ratio;
	 // console.log ("ratio  " + ratio) ;
	  }
    else
        eccentricAnomaly = eAo;
   }
    return eccentricAnomaly 
} 
function eccentricToTrueAnomaly(e, E) {
 // http://mmae.iit.edu/~mpeet/Classes/MMAE441/Spacecraft/441Lecture19.pdf slide 8
	var trueAnomaly = 2 * Math.atan(Math.sqrt((1+e)/(1-e))* Math.tan(E/2));
	return trueAnomaly
}
   function updateTheDate() 
   { // Display the simulated date to the right of the model.
   //  epoch.setTime(epoch.getTime() + simSpeed * 86400)
	 if (simSpeed == 1) {
	   epoch.setDate(epoch.getDate() + 1) ;            // At maximum speed, increment calendar by a day for each clock-cycle.
	 } else {  epoch.setTime(epoch.getTime() + simSpeed * 24 * 3600000) ; }  // 24 hours * milliseconds in an hour * simSpeed 

//	 document.getElementById("modelDate").innerHTML = (epoch.getMonth() + 1) + "-" + epoch.getDate() + "-" + epoch.getFullYear() ;
   }

function updatePosition() 
	{  // With each tick of the clock, propagate the position and set the translation attribute.
	  // Update the position for the following array of objects.
	  var currentPosition = [] ;
      var deltaTime = 0 ;
	  
	  for (var hB in heavenlyBodies) {
	    
		var hbTAnomoly = heavenlyBodies[hB].trueAnomoly ;
	    currentPosition = heavenlyBodies[hB].propagate(hbTAnomoly) ;  // Determine the current position.
		
	    var Xpos = currentPosition[0] ;
	    var Ypos = currentPosition[1] ;
	    var Zpos = currentPosition[2] ;
	    var hBName = heavenlyBodies[hB].name;   // get the name of the current object and update translation
		
		curObj = scene.getObjectByName(hBName) ;
		curObj.position.set (Xpos, Ypos, Zpos) ;
		
	//	console.log(curObj.name + "  " + curObj.position.x + ",  " + curObj.position.y + ",  " + curObj.position.z  ) ;
		  
	 // Calculate mean motion n:
		 var n = (2 * Math.PI) / (heavenlyBodies[hB].period * 365.25) ;   // radians per day
		 
	 // Calculate Eccentric Anomaly E based on the orbital eccentricity and previous true anomaly:
	    var e = heavenlyBodies[hB].oE ;
		var f = heavenlyBodies[hB].trueAnomoly          // heavenlyBodies[hB].trueAnomoly ;
        var eA = trueToEccentricAnomaly(e,f)            // convert from true anomaly to eccentric anomaly
		
	 // Calculate current Mean Anomaly	
		var m0 = eA - e * Math.sin(eA);	
	   
	 // deltaTime = (Math.abs(m0/n) - heavenlyBodies[hB].time) * simSpeed
    //  deltaTime = Math.abs(m0/n) * simSpeed
	    deltaTime = simSpeed * n

	 // Update Mean anomaly by adding the Mean Anomaly at Epoch to the mean motion * delaTime
         var mA = deltaTime + m0
		
		heavenlyBodies[hB].time = heavenlyBodies[hB].time +  deltaTime // increment timer

        eA = meanToEccentricAnomaly (e, mA) 
        var trueAnomaly = eccentricToTrueAnomaly(e, eA) 
		heavenlyBodies[hB].trueAnomoly = trueAnomaly
		
//    console.log(hBName + " time = " +  heavenlyBodies[hB].time + "  delta time " + dt)		
//	  console.log(hBName + " eccentric anomaly " + E + " sin(f) " + sinf + " cos(f) " + cosf )
//	  console.log(hBName + " mean anomaly " + mA + " eccentric anomaly " + eA ) 		
//    console.log (hBName + " trueAnomaly = " + trueAnomaly + "   true Anomaly  " + heavenlyBodies[hB].trueAnomoly + "  mean motion = " + n) ;
//	  console.log(hBName + " eccentricity " + e + " true anomaly " + f + " Eccentric anomaly " + eA + " Mean anomaly " + m0 + " mean motion " + n) 	 
	  }
	  updateTheDate() ;
	  
	};

/*----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------*
 *                            {--- Global variables --}                                         *
 *----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------*/
var epoch = new Date('December 9, 2014');  // start the calendar 
var simSpeed = 0.75 ;                        // value from the scroll control
var solid = false;                        // start simulation with solid rendering of orbits
var solidLabels = false;                  // start simulation with solid rendering of Labels

// Specify trajectories' sMA, oI, aP, oE, aN, mAe, Sidereal <-- refer to Trajectory constructor.
// Orbital elements source: http://www.met.rdg.ac.uk/~ross/Astronomy/Planets.html#rates
// Orbital period source: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_period
// Mean Anomoly at epoch for planets http://farside.ph.utexas.edu/teaching/celestial/Celestial/node34.html
// Source: http://neo.jpl.nasa.gov/cgi-bin/neo_elem?type=PHA;hmax=all;max_rows=20;action=Display%20Table;show=1&sort=moid&sdir=ASC
```

```
@prefix : <https://purl.org/space-ontology/ssao.owl> .
@prefix owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> .
@prefix rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> .

@prefix ssao: <https://purl.org/space-ontology/ssao.owl#> .
@base <https://purl.org/space-ontology/ssao.owl> .

<https://purl.org/space-ontology/ssao.owl> rdf:type owl:Ontology ;
                                            owl:imports <http://protege.stanford.edu/plugins/owl/dc/protege-dc.owl> ;
                                            <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/contributor> """Daniel A. O'Neil (NASA, Marshall Spaceflight Center)
daniel.a.oneil@nasa.gov
https://github.com/daoneil/"""@en ,
                                                                                          "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                            <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                      """Robert John Rovetto

rrovetto@terpalum.umd.edu
http://ontospace.wordpress.com
https://github.com/rrovetto/"""@en ;
                                            <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """The Space Situational Awareness ontology (SSAO) is an ontology for describing the concepts, data, knowledge, objects, events, and interactions of interest in space situational awareness (SSA) for the astronautics and astronomy. 

It formally represent activities and objects in the orbital space environment surrounding a celestial body such as Earth. It also represents the social and technological infrastructure supporting those activities. It expresses our knowledge of these entities, the processes by which we attain that knowledge, together with requisite data and infrastructure. 

The ontology defines categories, relationships, and their instances to capture both generic and specific domain knowledge of the target universe of discourse--the SSA domain (sometimes called 'space domain'). The ontology vocabulary can serve as metadata, semantically annotating data about satellites, as well as the orbital and ground systems supporting them. Defined terms can serve as a standard vocabulary for the community, or contribute to development of (inter)national standards. The project aims for a systematic, accurate and neutral development of ontologies and terminologies that are computable.  

SSA involves past, present and predictive knowledge about the orbital and near space environment, and the processes through which we attain that knowledge and associated data. For example, objects of interest include spacecraft orbiting Earth, datasets about their orbits and motion, and information about the data sources and associated entities. Activities of interest include observation, detection, tracking and identification, as well as the prediction (and simulation) of spacecraft future trajectories. This involves collecting, processing, analyzing and disseminating data from various sources, such as ground-based sensors.  The SSA domain is therefore tentatively construed to include the orbital space and near-space environments, occurrences therein, cataloged data about these entities and associated general knowledge (e.g., scientific laws or principles of astrodynamics).  

The project aims for systematic, accurate and neutral development of these ontologies and terminologies.  

Some purposes and goals of the ontology include: 
(1) To accurately represent objects in orbit, their orbits, and SSA data, processes, actors, and infrastructure.
(2) To support safe spaceflight and space situational awareness.
(3) To provide metadata to link, search, and retrieve data and information systems. 
(4) To provide a semantic layer for databases such as space object catalogs, and information systems, annotating the contained data elements to describe their meaning.
(5) To provide a standard, neutral, widely-applicable and common vocabulary, ontology suite, and knowledge model for the global community.
(6) To develop classifications of space objects such as spacecraft, orbital debris, etc.
(7) To provide a reference model that can be extended by more specialized ontologies.
(8) To be used in academia, industry, and gov't, including university projects, agencies such as NASA, organizations in private sector, mil. projects, and international standards development. 
(9) To explore various applications of semantic technology and artificial intelligence (AI) for astronautics.
(10) To provide an ontological model that can serve as an educational tool for the target domain.

The SSAO is based on [1] \"An Ontological Architecture for Orbital Debris Data” by Robert J. Rovetto, published 6 August 2015 in Earth Science Informatics (DOI: 10.1007/s12145-015-0233-3). It, and the ontology of SSA, was discuss in [2] “Preliminaries of a Space Situational Awareness Ontology”, by R.J.Rovetto and T.S. Kelso, in Advances in Astronautical Sciences, and presented at the 26th AAS Space Flight Mechanics meeting. 

The SSAO is a living work, and is in-progress. This particular file was created circa 2013-2016. No claims to completeness are made, and all content is subject to change.

Persons and organizations interested in sponsoring development, contributing to development, using the latest version, or working together, are enouraged to make contact with the author at rrovetto@terpalum.umd.edu or ontologos[at]yahoo[dot]com"""@en ;

Not authorized for commercial use unless explicitly negotiated with the copyright holder, creator or author. Attribution is required.

This work/ontology is provided by the authors and copyright holders \"AS IS\" and any express or implied warranties, including, but not limited to, the implied warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose are disclaimed. An example citation is: 
\"The Space Situational Awareness Ontology\", OWL format, version X.Y (2015), Robert J. Rovetto\". It may be supplemented with additional information such as \"See also https://purl.org/space-ontology. See also 'Preliminaries of a Space Situational Awareness Ontology', R.J.Rovetto, and T.S.Kelso (2016), in Advances in Astronautics.\""""@en ;
                                            <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/source> <https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/1606/1606.01924.pdf> ,
                                                                                     "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12145-015-0233-3"@en ;
                                            <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/title> "The Space Situational Awareness Ontology (SSAO)"@en ;
                                            rdfs:seeAlso <https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/1704/1704.01014.pdf> ,
                                                         <https://github.com/rrovetto/space-situational-awareness-domain-ontology> ,
                                                         <https://ntrs.nasa.gov/search.jsp?R=20200000988> ,
                                                         <https://purl.org/space-ontology> ,
                                                         <https://purl.org/space-ontology/ssao> ,
                                                         "http://www.univelt.com/book=5920"@en ;
                                            owl:versionInfo "0.5"@en ;
                                            <https://purl.org/space-ontology/About_the_Creator> """Robert John Rovetto (New York, United States of America) is a formal ontologist, modeler and researcher with a focus area of knowledge modeling for space. Another focus area is abstract, foundational, methodological, and ethical topics in ontology design, development, and use. At the time of this writing, he actively searches PhD study opportunities for this and other projects. He also gives extensive volunteering to both knowledge/semantic modeling groups, standards organizations, spaceflight committees, and emergency response organizations. A lifelong learner, some varied interests are listed at the end of the following.

Contact: 
rrovetto@terpalum.umd.edu, ontologos[at]yahoo[dot]com, robert.rovetto@amu.apus.edu
 
B.A., University of Maryland (UMD). 
M.A., State University of New York.
Coursework in Space Studies, American Military University (APUS)

Member of NASA Datanauts (2017-present):
https://open.nasa.gov/explore/datanauts/2017/spring/

Research Affiliate, Center for Orbital Debris Education & Research, Univ. of Maryland (2016-present).

Member of International Astronautical Federation, AIAA, CCSDS.

GoogleScholar publications webpage:
https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=jTkGEiMAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra

Project pages: 
https://github.com/rrovetto/
https://purl.org/space-ontology
https://ontospace.wordpress.com/

ResearchGate page:
www.researchgate.net/profile/Robert_Rovetto

Selected Goals:
1) To continue my education via a studentship.
2) To work for a space organization, such as NASA.
3) To develop ontologies, knowledge models, and terminologies for NASA and similar organizations (in industry, private sector, academia, government, etc.).
4) To find formal collaborations, sponsors, and contributors for this and related ontology projects.

Selected Areas of Interest: knowledge representation and reasoning, formal ontology, astronautics, space situational awareness, orbital debris, AI for astronautics, philosophy, space policy, maritime safety, maritime search & rescue, small-boat operations, foundational ontology topics."""@en ;
                                            <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Desiderata> """The following are desired to sustainably develop this and related works. Please contact the author at rrovetto@terpalum.umd.edu if you'd like to offer any of the following, or otherwise. 

(1) Sponsorship, or other funded opportunities
(2) Formal work collaborations
(3) A PhD study opportunity for the author to sustainable realize the project vision in a stable and mentored educational setting.
(4) Technical expertise and contributions to help with development, and help achieve technical desiderata such as (7-10) below.
(5) Subject-matter experts to help with subject coverage, modeling, and domain content verification.
(6) Application areas, and use-cases, for the ontology(s).
(7) Users of the ontology(s).

Technical desiderata includes:
(7) A graphical-user interface to dynamically search and display terms, definitions, semantic triples, and interactive graph of the ontology. 
(8) A hosting platform.
(9) Datasets to apply the ontology.
(10) Interfacing data and ontology models 
(11) Data sets 
(12) misc.

The project is open to ideas for application and innovation."""@en ;
                                            <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """The ontology is under development. This particular file represents an incomplete version.

A non-exhaustive list of tasks to be completed include the following (1-7, below). Please contact the author (rrovetto@terpalum.umd.edu) if you are interested in sponsoring, formally collaborating or contributing to development toward realize the project vision.

(1) Identifiers.
All constructs in the ontology (entities, classes, properties, individuals, etc.) are being assigned (i) Identifiers, and (ii) both preferred display labels and alternative or synonymous labels in natural language for human readability. It is anticipated that identifiers will direct to descriptive webpages, or to ontology source files (e.g., OWL files) on GitHub or elsewhere. The IRI's in this particular file may not be active at the time of this application with the NASA Ontology Oriented Orrery (Dr.O'Neil, NASA MSFC).

(2) Definitions & Formalization.
All ontology constructs or terms (e.g. labels) will list associated natural language definitions, and computable definitions. Constraints, axioms and rules are will be asserted, which will support automated inference.

Note: In this file, some constructs may display more than one definition/description, or none. Metadata, and OWL Annotations Properties, will be asserted to specify the type of definition where necessary.

(3) Modeling Alternatives.
Alternative modeling approaches are being explored. For example, Object vs. Data Properties of a similar concept, reflecting modeling attributes and their quantitative values.

(4) Modularization
Portions of the ontology will be modularized into their own reusable ontologies. They can then be imported into other ontology files, such as a master SSAO owl file, or an an external ontology. This reflects a modular ontology architecture according to which the target domain is delineated into sub-domains for more efficient computation, management, and reuse.

(5) Scope & Domain Coverage.
The scope of the SSAO may change. Alternative delineations of the domain may result in a more narrow scope. All modules are intended to be interconnected for a unified and holistic representational framework for the overarching universe of discourse of the space domain.

(6) Knowledge Representation & Reasoning (KRR).
It is anticipated/desired that the ontology will be implemented in more than one KRR language.

(7) Natural Languages
The current language is English, and translation into multiple languages is desired. 

Please contact the author if you're interested in contributing to development, using the ontology(s), or more recent versions."""@en ;
                                            <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Disclaimer> """The SSAO, in general, is a living work and all content is subject to revision. This including, but is not limited to title, scope, ontology constructs (classes, properties, individuals, metadata), structure, definitions, documentation, etc. 

This is a draft, an incomplete file version, circa 2013-2016. No claims to completeness are made, and it is presented \"as is\". No warranty.
Please contact the author if interested in more recent versions or interested in supporting development."""@en ;
                                            <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Editor> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                            <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Scope> """The SSAO aims to formally represent entities in, our knowledge of, and data about, the orbital space environment surrounding a celestial body, and occurrences therein. This includes how and from where we acquire that data and information.

It is primarily intended to ontologically represent such things as the orbits of satellites in outer space, the objects themselves (including their parts and features), how they move or behave, the physical and social infrastructure involved in observing and predicting the motion of those objects, the organizations involved, the observation and predictive activities themselves as well as the resultant data, and relevant scientific principles. A special focus is on spacecraft and orbital debris.

The scope of this ontology is that of the SSA or space domain. At the specific instance level, this encompasses the near-Earth environment and the actual phenomena therein, including particular satellites (e.g., the International Space Station, asteroids, etc.), their inter-relationships, how they interact; data about them at a particular time (and over time), and the activities generating that data, and knowledge and situational awareness of the space environment. At a generic level, this involves capturing general knowledge of the orbital and near-space environment (including phenomena therein) for any astronomical body. Combined, this yields what has been called a domain knowledge model, reference model, semantic model, knowledge graph, etc.

The scope more precisely includes the following. 
(a) observation, detection, tracking, identification, and prediction of (artificial and natural) objects, and their past, present and future position and motion in orbit. 
(b) the agents engaging in these activities of achieving actionable SSA.
(c) the infrastructure and resources agents use in SSA-relevant activities and missions, e.g., sensor networks; data processing systems; ground, launch, and space segments.
(d) Data, such as sensor data, and spacecraft telemetry data, collected from various activities and processes.
(e) Data flow processes, e.g., from sensor to spacecraft operator.
(f) Spacecraft and orbital debris, as well as their parts, properties, behaviors, etc.
(g) Events, actions, and processes occurring in orbit, e.g., collisions, spacecraft maneuvers, etc.
(h) predictions and beliefs about current or future space object positions and trajectories
(i) Concepts and scientific principles of astrodynamics, orbital dynamics, etc.
(i) etc.

The scope is subject to change."""@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Intended_Meaning_of_Ontology_Construct
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Intended_Meaning_of_Ontology_Construct> rdf:type owl:AnnotationProperty ;
                                                                         <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                                         rdfs:comment """This annotation provides, in natural language, the intended meaning or purpose of an ontology construct/element being created, i.e., the symbol structure which takes the form of some set of symbols (whether a human readible phrase or an opaque alphanumeric identifier) and which is associated a human-readible label (distinct from the construct being created).
 
Note: Examples of ontology constructs/elements (or symbol structures) are Classes, Object Properites and Annotation Properties in Protege.

The annotation note should be presented in a way most expressive to the author to maximize comprehensibility and expression of intended meaning/purpose. In this way, this annotaiton expresses descriptive meta-level information combined with object level information, which should match with any definition of the associated label for the given construct.

This reflects a distinction between the description of the construct (the class, relation, or indvidiual), and the lexical definition of the label it is given. 

rdfs:comment and dc:description may be similar, but the idea here is to make the above distinction explicit, i.e., to show the finer detail. 

Consider this: a desription of the term 'dog' (where 'dog' is the value of, say, rdfs:label or skos:prefLabel for the given class construct) may be \"a three-lettered word that...\", whereas the definition of 'dog' may be \"a three-legged mammal that...\". 

Therefore, the display/preferred/rendered label (i.e., term) for the construct should have a meaning (definition) that matches it. The two should match--they should express similar, if not the same, intended meaning.

If, however, a label definition is not the same as this, then a definition annotation should provide a more structured definition.

This annotation provides a human-readible statement of the intended meaning or purpose of an ontology element/construct/symbol structure or the human-readible label of that element, i.e., expressing a fundamental understanding of its semantics."""@en ;
                                                                         rdfs:label "Intended Meaning of the Ontology Construct"@en ;
                                                                         <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Further development needed. 

Disambiguate between Intended Meaninig, Definition, and Clarifying Remark annotations."""@en ;
                                                                         <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Example> """This class is intended as a category for all dogs.

NOTE: contrast this will a definition of 'dog' which may be 'a four-legged mammal...'."""@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Natural_Language_Definition_of_Label
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Natural_Language_Definition_of_Label> rdf:type owl:AnnotationProperty ;
                                                                       <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                                       rdfs:comment """A statement, in natural language, expressing the intended meaning of the label (term or word) assigned to the selected ontology element/concept/construct (class, relation, indivdiual, etc.). It is a definition of the preferred or rendered/displayed label.

In other words, the annotation provides the definition of the label assigned to the selected ontology class, relation, or indivdiual."""@en ;
                                                                       rdfs:label "Natural Language Definition of Label"@en ;
                                                                       <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Further development needed.

This annotation provides, in natural language, the intended meaning of the preferred label (term) of the selected ontology construct (i.e., class, relation, indvidiual,, etc.). It is a definition of at least the preferred label term, if not alternative or synonymous label terms.

This reflects a distinction between the description of the construct, and the definition of the label it is given. rdfs:ccomment and dc:description may be seen as similar, but the idea is to make the distinction explicit, i.e., to show the finer detail. Consider this: a desription of the term 'dog' may be 'a three-lettered word that...', whereas the definition of 'dog' may be 'a three-legged mammal that...'. 

Therefore, the preferred/rendered label (i.e., term) for the construct should have a meaning (definition) that matches it. The two should match--they should express similar, if not the same, intended meaning.

If, however, a label definition is not the same as this, then a definition annotation should provide a more structured definition.

Examples of ontology elements or constructs are Classes, Object Properites and Annotation Properties in Protege."""@en ;
                                                                       rdfs:subPropertyOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Definition> .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Preferred_Label
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Preferred_Label> rdf:type owl:AnnotationProperty ;
                                                  <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                  <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """The preferred label (term) of the given entity/concept.

Where a given entity/concept in the ontology has alternative labels (labels or terms that communicate/express the same intended meaninig, e.g., equivalent or synonymous terms) a preferred one will be selected."""@en ;
                                                  rdfs:comment """The Preferred Label annotation indicates the preferred natural language label (term or word phrase) for a particular ontology construct (class, property, individual, etc.). It will most likely be the label indicated by the rdfs:label annotation. It may be composed of one or more words. It can be understood as the name of the given intended meaning or definition.

The preferred label, and rdfs:label, should have a form that most closely expresses, matches, and is most easily understood as expressing, the intended meaning of associated (or corresponding) ontology construct. For example, a label composed of multiple words should have words whose meaning is easily understood and whose arrangement most closely expresses the intended meaning of the whole construct.

In other words, the preferred label, and rdfs:label, should capture the natural language definition as closely as possible.

The intended meaning of a created class, relation or indvidiual should corresponds closely with its preferred label. 

The preferred label should have a form that most closely corresponds to, and is most easily understood as expressing, the intended meaning."""@en ;
                                                  rdfs:label "Preferred Label"@en .

###  http://www.semanticweb.org/rrovetto/ontologies/2014/space-situational-awareness-ontology#has_orbital_eccentricity
<http://www.semanticweb.org/rrovetto/ontologies/2014/space-situational-awareness-ontology#has_orbital_eccentricity> rdf:type owl:DatatypeProperty ,
                                                                                                                             owl:FunctionalProperty ;
                                                                                                                    rdfs:range [ rdf:type rdfs:Datatype ;
                                                                                                                                 owl:onDatatype xsd:decimal ;
                                                                                                                                 owl:withRestrictions ( [ xsd:minInclusive 0.0
                                                                                                                                                        ]
                                                                                                                                                        [ xsd:maxInclusive 1.0
                                                                                                                                                        ]
                                                                                                                                                      )
                                                                                                                               ] ;
                                                                                                                    <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                                                                                    <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """This data property is a binary predicate expressing the eccentricity of the orbit of an object in its orbit at a particular time.

An orbit can have only one eccentricity at a time for a given time.

The possible values of orbital eccentricty range from 0 to 1, and therefore this data property can have the same decimal value range."""@en ,
                                                                                                                                                                  "This data property represents a binary relation expressing the eccentricity of an orbiting object in its orbit at a particular time" ;
                                                                                                                    rdfs:label "has_orbital_eccentricity"@en ;
                                                                                                                    <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "has orbit eccentricity value"@en .


###  http://www.semanticweb.org/rrovetto/ontologies/2014/space-situational-awareness-ontology#has_orbital_inclination
<http://www.semanticweb.org/rrovetto/ontologies/2014/space-situational-awareness-ontology#has_orbital_inclination> rdf:type owl:DatatypeProperty ;
                                                                                                                   rdfs:range [ rdf:type rdfs:Datatype ;
                                                                                                                                owl:oneOf [ rdf:type rdf:List ;
                                                                                                                                            rdf:first 0 ;
                                                                                                                                            rdf:rest [ rdf:type rdf:List ;
                                                                                                                                                       rdf:first 360 ;
                                                                                                                                                       rdf:rest rdf:nil
                                                                                                                                                     ]
                                                                                                                                          ]
                                                                                                                              ] ;
                                                                                                                   <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                                                                                   <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "The numeric value, in degrees, of the orbits inclination."@en ;
                                                                                                                   rdfs:label "has_orbital_inclination"@en ;

                                                        rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Classical_Keplerian_Orbital_Element> ;
                                                        <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;

                                                        <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "argument of periapsis"@en ;

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Argument_of_Perigee
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Argument_of_Perigee> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                      rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Argument_of_Periapsis> ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """Argument of Perigee desribes the orientation of an orbit in its orbital plane relative to Earth. 
It defines where the low point, perigee, of the orbit is with respect to the Earth's surface (https://spaceflight.nasa.gov/realdata/elements/).
It is the angle, measured in the direction of satellite motion, from the Ascending Node to Perigee.
It has values greater than 0 but less than 360 degrees.
The angle from line of nodes to satellite position vector.
It's value is undefined when orbital inclination is 0 or 180 degrees, or when orbtal eccentricity is 0.
It is represented by Greek lowercase omega."""@en ;
                                                      rdfs:label "argument of perigee"@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Central_Body
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Central_Body> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                               <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                               <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "The Central Body is the most massive of the bodies in an orbital system."@en ;
                                               rdfs:label "central body"@en ;
                                               <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Central Body"@en ,
                                                                                                   "Central Mass"@en ,
                                                                                                   "Primary"@en ,
                                                                                                   "Primary Body"@en ,
                                                                                                   "Primary Mass"@en ;
                                               <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> "The central body (or central mass, or primary body) of a multi-body gravitational system (an orbital system, e.g., solar system) is the more massive of the bodies in the system. In other words, it is the body around which all other bodies in the system orbit. The concept of a central body (or central mass) thereby may reflect a context-specific situation. It may be a relative concept, and always in relation to one or more other entities, and with respect to an observer. A central body is considered relative to a given orbital system, i.e. a specific set of bodies. The central body of our solar system is the Sun, but is the Earth of the Earth-moon system. It can therefore be ontologically modeled in a couple of ways. One is as a role played by a celestial body. A body that is assigned the role of central body by an observer."@en .

                                                                                        ]
                                                                                      ) ;

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Classical_Keplerian_Orbital_Element
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Classical_Keplerian_Orbital_Element> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                                      rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Property> ;
                                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """In general, the orbital elements are the properties, features, measurable quantities, or parameters required to identify an orbit, and describe the motion of a satellite in orbit. The orbital elements desribe the motion of satellites in an orbit. In general, 6 parameters are needed to uniquely define an orbit and a satellite's position within the orbit. 

The Keplerian (or classical) element describes the size, shape and orientation of an orbit, as well as the location of satellite in the given orbit.

Orbital elements are parameters to describe an orbit.
An orbital element set is a set of quantities specified relative to to a coordinate sysetm and reference frame to describe the orbit of a satelltie. Position and velocity (2 elements) are needed to define an orbit. WIth these elements, a satellites past and future position and velocity may be predicted. 3 parameters each are needed to describe position and velocity in 3-dimensional space. Thus, 6 parameters are needed for an element set.

They describe non-inertial orbital trajectories of the orbiting bodies."""@en ;
                                                                      rdfs:comment """The orbital elements, or specific value ranges thereof, may serve as necessary conditions, or identity conditions, of individual orbits.
An element set has elements as parts.Those elements will have particular values for particular measures of a satellites orbital motion at a time."""@en ,
                                                                                   "There are many ways to mathematically desccribe an orbit."@en ;
                                                                      rdfs:label "Classical Keplerian Orbital Element"@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Gravitational_Orbit
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Gravitational_Orbit> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                      rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbit> ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                                "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """A curved path desribed by an object under the influence of gravitation. 
The path desribed by one body revolving around another. (See Merriam Webster's Dictiionary). 

Gravitational Orbits are orbits bound by gravitation, and determined by the combination of gravity and the motion of the orbiting object.
Gravitational orbits are gravitationally-bound orbits.
The path of an object orbting a gravitationally-binding mass.
The gravitationally-induced path of an object.
The path traveled by an object bound by gravitation around another object.
The path or motion of an entity (the orbiter) around another entity (the orbited / central entity / central body) due to gravitation. The gravitationally-induced path or motion of an entity aroumd another gravitationally-binding entity."""@en ;
                                                      rdfs:comment "The types of orbits of interest for the ontology are orbits bound by gravitation, i.e., orbits of objects in astronomical space (the microgravity environment). Therefore, gravitational orbits are orbits that are gravitationally-bound, or the orbits of objects that are gravitationally bound, by some larger mass. The category terms 'Gravitaitonal orbit', 'Astronomical Orbit', or 'Celestial Orbit' are more precise than 'Orbit', but the latter is context-specifically understood to mean the former."@en ;
                                                      rdfs:label "gravitational orbit"@en ;
                                                      <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Astronomical Orbit"@en ,
                                                                                                          "Celestial Orbit"@en ,
                                                                                                          "Gravitationally-bound Orbit"@en ,
                                                                                                          "Orbit"@en ;
                                                      <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> "Ongoing development. ###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Measurement

                                              rdfs:label "measurement"@en ;
                                              <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Disambiguate activity of measuring from the measurement (as in the numeric value, that may be the result of the activity).

Measurements are essential to SSA. Observations involve taking measurements, and therefore yield measurement data. The relationship between these and other related entities should be represented in the ontology.

A particular measurement indicates a value of the property of some property-bearing subject or object. For example, a measurement of the mass of an object is a specific value (e.g., 500 grams) for the mass property of the object."""@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbit
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbit> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                        <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                        <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "The path desribed or traced by a body revolving around another."@en ;
                                        rdfs:label "orbit"@en ;
                                        rdfs:seeAlso "\"The path described by one body in its revolution about another\" (Merriam Webster's Collegiate Dictionary)"@en ;
                                        <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Description_of_Class> "This is a category for the various kinds of orbits, such as orbits of astronommical bodies, orbits of subatomic particles, etc."@en ;
                                        <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Although the intended concept to represent in this ontology is the orbits in astronomical space, i.e. gravitationally-determined orbits, the term 'orbit' is broader (e.g., the orbits of subatomic particles). One way to differentiate them is by the binding forces. Therefore it will be more precise to use 'orbit' as a catch-all term, and a more specific term for the target orbits.

The broadest concept to express is that of one thing or entity revolving around another. This covers both micro and macroscopic objects (such as spacecraft and planets), as well as centers of gravity.
Note also that dictionary definitions of 'orbit' provide various senses.

Both astronautical literature (including SSA and astronomy) and the non-specialist, often use 'orbit' to mean orbits of object in outer space. This ontology work will explore formally linking context-specific terms to more precise terms that may be asserted in the ontology.

Formal definitions, at least from a philosophical perspective, are under development by the author/ontology-creator (as of approx. 2012)."""@en ,
                                                                                                  "R.J.Rovetto's (the author) orbit type ontology."@en ;
                                        <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Editor> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                        <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Scope> "Various types of orbit at various scales or granularity, from subatomic particles (i.e. particle orbits) to astronomical objects (i.e., gravitational or celestial orbits)."@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbit_Data
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbit_Data> rdf:type owl:Class ;

[1], \"An Ontological Architecture for Orbital Debris Data\" (Rovetto, R.J. 6 Aug 2015, Earth Science Informatics)."""@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Eccentricity
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Eccentricity> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                       rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Classical_Keplerian_Orbital_Element> ;
                                                       <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                                       <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """Eccentricity desribes the shape of an orbit, specifically how much the orbit deviates from a circle. It is represented with  the symbol 'e'.
Closed orbits have an eccentricity greater or equal to 0 but less than 1.
Open orbits have an eccentricity greater or equal to 1.
It is the ratio of half the foci separation (c) to the semi-major axis.
For elliptical orbits it can be calcultated by the apoapsis minus periapsis divided by twice the semimajor axis (or the apoapsis plus the periapsis)."""@en ;
                                                       rdfs:label "orbital eccentricity"@en ;
                                                       <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Orbit Eccentricity"@en ;
                                                       <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Clarifying_Note> """Defines the shape of the orbit.
Describes the tilt of the orbit"""@en .

                                                  <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                  rdfs:label "Orbital Element"@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Event
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Event> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                          "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                rdfs:comment "Orbital events are events occurring in an orbit about a celestial body."@en ;
                                                rdfs:label "orbital event"@en ;
                                                <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Disambiguate between orbital events, orbital activities, and orbital processes.
Example: an Orbital Activity is an Activity, occuring in orbit, in which an Actor/Agent engages or participates."""@en ,
                                                                                                          "R.J.Rovetto's orbital event ontology."@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Inclination
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Inclination> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                      rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Classical_Keplerian_Orbital_Element> ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """Orbital inclination describes the tilt of the orbital plane.
It defines the orientation of the orbit with respect to the Earth's equator. 
Equatorial inclinations are 0 or 180 degrees.
Prograde are greater or equal to 0 but less than 90 degrees.
Polar are 90 degrees.
Retrograde are greater than 90 but less than 180 degrees.
It is represented with the symbol 'i'."""@en ;
                                                      rdfs:comment "This is a class intended to represent inclination of gravitaitonal orbits, or objects in orbit."@en ;
                                                      rdfs:label "orbital inclination"@en ;
                                                      <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Orbit Inclination"@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Path

                                               <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                         "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                               <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "A path through space or space-time that an object describes in its motion around another. The spatial path an object traces or follows in orbit about a celestial body or center of gravity. The spaital or spatio-temporal path an object in orbital motion traverses."@en ;
                                               rdfs:label "Orbital Path"@en ;
                                               <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Development ongoing.
A category whose instances may be the particular spatial extent or spatio-temporal region traced, followed or occupied by an object in orbt over a particular period of time."""@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Period

                                                 <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Period"@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Plane
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Plane> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Geometric_Entity> ;
                                                <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "The two-dimensional plane upon which the path of an orbiting object is projected in order to help desrcibe the objects orbit and motion."@en ;
                                                rdfs:label "orbital plane"@en ;
                                                <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Orbital Plane"@en ;

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Property
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbital_Property> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                   rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Physical_Property> ;
                                                   <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                             "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                   <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "A property, feature, parameter, quality, or characteristic of an orbit."@en ;
                                                   rdfs:label "Orbital Property"@en ;
                                                   <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Description_of_Class> "This class is intended to categorize various feature of orbits, e.g., the classical orbital elements, apoapsis, perigee, etc."@en ;
                                                   <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Ongoing development.

The orbital features, such as apogee, can have corresponding numeric measurement values (captured by OWL Data Properties such as has_orbital_property_value, has_Apogee_measurement_value, has_quantitative_measurement, etc.). 

In this way, an Orbit or a Spacecraft class or instance can be related to the Orbital Property and the specific (instance) value of the property at a given time.
Example: Orbit has_Apogee Apogee and Apogee has_Apogee_value 2000 km.

Alternatively, if no property classes are desired, then OWL Data Properties may suffice. The value would take a particular data type (integer, etc.). Example: Orbit has_Apogee_meaurement_value 2000 km.

Likewise can be done for the dates and times of events, e.g. mission execution event, orbital maneuver event, launch date, orbital conjunction time, etc."""@en ;
                                                   <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Example> "Orbital eccentricity, inclination, semimajor axis, etc."@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Primary_Satellite
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Primary_Satellite> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                    rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Orbit_Determination_Concept> ;
                                                    <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                    <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """The term 'primary satellite' typically signifies the object of interest (or focus) in conjunction assessment. Secondary satellites are objects in relative motion to the primary, and which may collide with the primary.

The concept of a primary (or secondary) satellite in activities, such as conjunction assessment, can be modeled as roles played by a physical object in orbit. 

These concepts reflect a relative aspect, but does not reflect any objective aspect of the objects (e.g., a spacecraft) in question. An object is primary relative to the observer and their activity of assessing its likelihood of colliding with other objects.

Similarly, 'primary body' in celestial mechanics typically refers to the celestial body, in an orbital system, with the largest mass."""@en ;
                                                    rdfs:label "primary satellite"@en ;
                                                    <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Primary Object"@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Reference_Entity

For example, a coordinate system is an abstract mathematical construct that is often projected onto a material object such as the Earth for the purpose of identifying the relative position of nearby objects."""@en ;

a space object in orbit (about Earth or another celestial body).
a space object orbiting another object
a space object in orbital motion around another object"""@en ;

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Right_Ascension_of_the_Ascending_Node
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Right_Ascension_of_the_Ascending_Node> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                                        rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Classical_Keplerian_Orbital_Element> ;
                                                                        <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """RAAN describes the rotation of the orbital plane about a central body such as Earth. It is the angle, measured eastward, from the vernal equanox to the ascending node.
It defines the location of the ascending and descending orbit locations with respect to the Earth's equatorial plane (https://spaceflight.nasa.gov/realdata/elements/).
It has values greater or equal to 0 but less than 360 degrees.
It's value is undefined for equatorial orbits, i.e., when inclination is 0 or 180 degrees.
It is a measure of the angle from the x-axis of the reference coordinate system to the line of nodes. E.g.,: the angle from vernal equinox direction to the line of nodes."""@en ;
                                                                        rdfs:label "right ascension of the ascending node"@en ;
                                                                        <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "RAAN"@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Satellite_Catalog_Number
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Satellite_Catalog_Number> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                           rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Identifier> ;
                                                           <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ;
                                                           rdfs:label "satellite catalog number"@en ;
                                                           <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Distinguish between the catalog number used in particular catalogs such as the US DoD SATCAT, and the generic category of Spacecraft Catalog Number.

Consider different modeling approaches. One, use a generic 'Identifier' class together with a relation such as 'is-assigned-by' to link the particular spacecraft number to the database, organization or agent that assigns and owns the number. 
Example: 
Spacecraft-001 has-Identifier A001
A001 is-instance-of Identifier
A001 is-assigned-by COSPAR.

Two, a hierachy of spacecraft identifier clases, each of which are for specific organizations or databases.
Example:
Spacecraft-001 has-COSPAR-ID A001
A001 is-instance-of COSPAR_ID
COSPAR_ID is-a-subclass-of Identifier."""@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Sensor_Observation
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Sensor_Observation> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                     rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Observation> ;
                                                     <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                               "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                     <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """A sensor observation (dataset) consists of the position and often the velocity of an object in outerspace taken at a particular time and relative to the obseving sensor.
As a data set of recorded quantities, a particular observation is an instance."""@en ;
                                                     rdfs:comment """\"Observation\" in the space situational awareness, astronautics, and astonomy communities is sometimes used ambiguously. It often refers to data collected by a sensor. 
An observation in the SSA community, for example, is typically understood as sensor data, or a dataset provided by sensors observing outerspace. A particular observation is a detection of an object in orbit."""@en ;
                                                     rdfs:label "sensor observation"@en ;
                                                     <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "observation"@en ;
                                                     <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Further development is needed to model what various astroautical groups call 'observations'. Differentiate between data, datasets, the activity of observation, the result of the observation (e.g. a dataset), etc.

Consider modeling observations as such... 
Distinguish between at least the act of observing, the observer, and the product of the activity. The observation of the orbital environments yields a dataset about detected objects in that environment. 

More precisely, the activity of observing is enacted by a space-based or ground-based sensor (an actor). That activity yields a observation dataset, i.e., a dataset recorded by the sensor. An observation often involves measuring some phenomena. Measurements an the activity of measuring should be represented, including the quantitative elements, such as units of distance and mass (e.g., meters and grams).

The genesis of the observation itself begins with electromagnetic energy being received by a sensor, recorded as data, processed, etc. That data may then be transitted from the sensor facility to another location (and actor).

Consider also an observation as a single event, as a single detection of an object in terms of azimuth and elevation relative to the sensor making the observation (see U.S. gov publication SD505)."""@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Environment
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Environment> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                    <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                              "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                    rdfs:label "Space Environment"@en ;
                                                    <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Astronomical Space Environment"@en ,
                                                                                                        "Outer space Environment"@en ,
                                                                                                        "Space Domain"@en ;
                                                    <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Description_of_Class> "This is a class intended to capture the astronomical environment, or the microgravity environment of outer space. Parts or portions of this environment may be characterized as subclasses, such as Near-Space Environment, and Orbital Space Environment. These subclasses would be relative or relational with respect to a celestial object or the reference body (such as a planet), or in reference to an agent such as an observer (person or sensor)."@en ;
                                                    <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> "Ongoing development."@en .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Mission
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Mission> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> <http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3835-7817> ,
                                                                                          "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                rdfs:label "Space Mission"@en ;
                                                rdfs:seeAlso """Robert Rovetto's Space Mission Ontology.
https://github.com/rrovetto/Space-Mission-Ontology"""@en ;
                                                <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#altLabel> "space mission"@en ;
                                                <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Alternative_Label> "Astronautical Mission"@en ,
                                                                                                    "Spaceflight Mission"@en ;
                                                <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Ongoing development.

As an activity or a temporally-extended entity, Space Missions (or Spaceflight Mission, or Astronautical Mission) is an activity in which at least one spacecraft engages, partcipates, enacts, etc.

Missions can have phases such as preparation phases, launch phase, orbit insertion phase, orbital phase, coasting phase, deorbiting phase,  landing phase, etc. Each phase may, in turn, involve or consist of activities enacted by specific actors (spacecraft, astronauts, etc.)"""@en .

<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Mission_Phase> rdf:type owl:Class ;

                                                                                                "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                      <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> """Part of the entire activity or process of a space mission. 
Part of a space mission, where space missions are described as a temporally occurring entity."""@en ;
                                                      rdfs:label "Space Mission Phase"@en .

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Object
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Object> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                               <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/creator> "Robert J. Rovetto"@en ;
                                               <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "an object located in outer space"@en ;
                                               rdfs:label "space object"@en ;
                                               rdfs:seeAlso "https://philpapers.org/archive/ROVSOO.pdf"@en ,
                                                            "https://philpapers.org/rec/ROVSOO"@en ;
                                               <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Development_Status_Note> """Problem: The category of 'space object' is not strictly necessary. Although the lexical term is often used in the spaceflight community, typcially informally, it is not necessarily recommended to denote typical meaning of artificial object in space, because the term is inherently broader and ambiguous. The intended meaning is typically more specific than the term itself, resulting in a mismatch. It does not reflect a stable ontological category. There is nothing in the term that singles out spacecraft as opposed to planets (planets are also space objects).  

If the criteria is location-based, then that meaning reflects an temporary or non-stable criterion: an object in outerspace may fall to Earth, which will no longer make it a space object. 

Solution 1: The concept of roles can be applied. Objects in outer space can be characterized as holding the Space Object Role at one time (e.g., when in Earth orbit), but not at another time (e.g., after landing on Earth's surface).

Solution 2: The concept of Space Object Contact can be used to group those objects in orbit that have been detected. 

Solution 3: Define Space Object to have no ontological (metaphysical) import.

See \"Space Object Ontology\" by Rovetto, R.J.,  https://philpapers.org/rec/ROVSOO
(a.k.a. \"Space Object Ontology and Taxonomy Development\")"""@en ,
                                                                                                         "Under development. There are various ways to categorize objects in outer space, and various permutations are being consider for this portion of the ontology (which will form an ontology file unto itself)."@en ;
                                               <https://purl.org/space-ontology/IRI_UUID_Shortname> "0faf8f8f_7c3b_41a5_ad17_a99c9b913e01" .


###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Object_Catalog
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Object_Catalog> rdf:type owl:Class ;

###  https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Segment
<https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Segment> rdf:type owl:Class ;
                                                rdfs:subClassOf <https://purl.org/space-ontology/Space_Mission_Segment> ;

                                                                                          "Robert John Rovetto"@en ;
                                                <http://purl.org/dc/elements/1.1/description> "A space mission, and the SSA domain, is often desribed as having segments: the ground segment, control segment, launch segment, space segment, user segment, etc. Each represents a grouping of sysetms, activities, and personnel that form part of and realize the overall mission, or SSA system."@en ;
```
